key_numbers.metric: Initial home care agency license application fee (nonrefundable; sent with the signed application packet, not after approval)
Annual license renewal fee; license term is one year and expires at midnight Dec. 31 (renewal and fee must be received by Dec. 31)
key_numbers.value: $510.00 per year. Every license expires at midnight Dec. 31 whatever the issue date, so a license issued mid-year needs a first $510 renewal received by Dec. 31 of that year; year one can carry two $510 payments. A renewal received after Jan. 1 takes effect only on the date received, which leaves a licensure gap.
DHSR publishes no fixed processing time ("not possible to establish specific time frames"); the applicant must complete all requirements within 12 months of DHSR receiving the application and fee
Proof of prior home care ownership/operation OR completion of DHSR-approved home care provider training; no license is issued until training is received (10A NCAC 13J .0903)

Any state license fee other than the official $510. Secondary sites cite $400, $500 or $560 and 60–90 day timelines, which conflict with the DHSR fee schedule [S3] and FAQ [S2].

Private-pay market size. CareScout's $30/hour is a statewide median for a combined homemaker/home health aide 'non-medical caregiver' category [S23], and metro-level prices were not retrieved. Senior IDY's $24–$35 range [S25] is secondary.
Current PCS beneficiary and unit counts under NC Medicaid Direct and Tailored Plans.
Several pages were retrieved via search excerpts only, so quotes should be re-checked against live pages before publication.
Raleigh-Cary BLS group means ($19.29 personal care and service, $20.28 healthcare support, $71.52 management) cited to S26. These were not re-verified and are not used in the customer text.

Alliance Health notice details (billing start 8/4/2026, re-adjudication of prior claims) cited to S10. They were not re-verified.

The modeled profit, break-even and cash figures. An independent rough recompute of the 60-client private-pay case gave about $6.5k–$9.4k a month against the stated $5,177. All figures were run at the $17.21 national aide wage and need re-running at the NC wage, with the relief-RN line and an overtime allowance.

configurations.label: Private-pay home care agency, 20 clients (RN owner-director, part-time scheduler)
configurations.notes: Smallest realistic start. The owner is a licensed health care practitioner (RN), so she or he qualifies as agency director under 10A NCAC 13J .1001 and also covers the RN supervision and plan-of-care home visits that DHSR requires [S2]. All clients pay privately at the CareScout NC median of $30/hour [S23]. Hours per client (80 per month, about 18 per week) are an operator estimate, well below the survey's 44-hour/week pricing basis. The model shows this size does not cover a $72,000 owner salary plus the required coverage. It is a starter size, not a recommended end state.

The vintage of that figure is not stated, and the NC-specific BLS OEWS May 2025 value was not retrieved, so confirm at bls.gov/oes (state = NC). The national median is $17.21 ($35,800 ÷ 2,080, May 2025) [S27] and was used in the earlier model run. The wage is far above the $7.25 NC minimum [S28]. Hours = 80 billable hours per client-month plus 4% paid non-billable time (travel, orientation). Both hours figures are operator estimates, so verify locally. Aide wage is the most sensitive input: each $1.00 per hour changes aide cost by about $97 per client-month with burden.

payroll_burden.notes: Payroll tax of 9% = employer FICA 7.65% plus NC unemployment tax at the 2026 beginning-employer rate of 1.0% on the first $34,200 per employee [S29], plus roughly 0.25% FUTA. FICA and FUTA are standard federal rates that are not in the source list. The new-employer UI rate holds for an initial period, then moves to experience rating (0.06%–5.76% in 2026) [S29]. Workers' comp at 5% is an operator estimate for home care class codes, because the NC class code and rate were not retrieved. Benefits at 3% are an operator estimate. Total burden is 17%. No overtime allowance is included: the model assumes no aide exceeds 40 hours a week. Third-party home care employers cannot use the FLSA companionship or live-in exemption (29 CFR 552.109), so hours over 40 a week must be paid at 1.5x. With 80 billable hours per client-month plus travel time across a pooled aide workforce, verify against actual schedules; a 3–6% allowance on aide wages is a reasonable sensitivity.

sections.executive_summary:
North Carolina has one license for a business that sends aides into homes. It is the **Home Care Agency license**, issued by the NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation (DHSR), Acute and Home Care Licensure and Certification Section, under G.S. 131E-135 through 131E-142 and the rules in 10A NCAC 13J [S1][S5]. In-home aide, companion, sitter, respite and homemaker services all count as home care under G.S. 131E-136(3), and operating without the license is prohibited by G.S. 131E-138 [S2]. A license for non-Medicare-certified home care does not need a Certificate of Need. The CON applies only to Medicare-certified home health [S2].

Start-up licensing is cheap and slow to predict. The initial application fee is **$510** (nonrefundable) and is sent with the signed application packet. Annual renewal is also **$510** and is due by December 31. Every license expires on December 31 whatever its issue date, so a license issued mid-year needs its first renewal that same year, and year one can carry two $510 payments [S3][S1][S2]. DHSR says it cannot publish processing time frames, but the applicant must finish every requirement within **12 months** of DHSR receiving the application and fee [S1][S2]. An applicant who has not previously owned or operated a home care agency must complete DHSR-approved training before a license can issue [S6][S2]. An RN must be available for supervision and consultation whenever aide services are being delivered, and the agency RN must make the plan-of-care home visit [S2]. That RN requirement is the main fixed cost the rules create.

Money comes from two streams:

- **Private pay.** CareScout's 2025 survey puts North Carolina's median non-medical in-home caregiver rate at **$30 per hour** ($5,720 per month on a 44-hour week) [S23].
- **NC Medicaid Personal Care Services (PCS) and CAP/DA.** NC Medicaid applied an **18% increase** effective August 1, 2026. State Plan PCS (code 99509, HA/HB) and CAP/C (S5125) went from $5.96 to **$7.03 per unit** [S8]. The increase covers NC Medicaid Direct and the CAP/C, CAP/DA and CAP/CD waivers [S8]. The bulletin table does not state the unit length. This report reads it as 15 minutes ($28.12 per hour), which is an inference to confirm on the NC Medicaid fee schedule (Section 4).

The financial result depends heavily on the aide wage, and the model has not yet been re-run at the North Carolina wage. The earlier run used the national aide median of $17.21 per hour [S27]. The only NC figure found is the NC Careers median of about **$15.02 per hour** (vintage not stated; the NC-specific BLS figure was not retrieved). At the $17.21 national wage, the best models were a **60-client private-pay agency** (about $5,177 per month, a 4.0% margin, break-even near 75.7% occupancy) and a **100-client Medicaid agency** (about $5,640 per month, 2.8%, break-even near 78.4%). Both took 13 to 15 months to a first profitable month and needed roughly $194,000 and $312,000 of cash. The 20- and 40-client private-pay agencies lost money. Moving to $15.02 lowers aide cost by about $213 per client-month, which by arithmetic alone adds roughly $11,500 per month at 54 clients and is large enough to change the 20- and 40-client loss results. The re-run must also include a relief RN for the 20-client owner-RN model and an overtime allowance. Treat every profit and cash figure as provisional (Section 8).
sections.service_model:
**Who is served.** Home care clients are mainly older adults and adults with disabilities who need help with bathing, dressing, toileting, meals, housekeeping and companionship at home. North Carolina's 65-and-older population was **2,038,854 in 2025 (about 18%)** and is projected to reach **2,996,376 by 2050** [S30]. CAP/DA covers adults aged 18 and over with disabilities who are at risk of institutionalization [S14]. The waiver serves adults 65 and older (no maximum age) and physically disabled adults 18 to 64 [S20].

**What the license covers.** The license covers in-home aide services, in-home companion, sitter and respite care, and homemaker services as defined in G.S. 131E-136(3) [S2]. This is non-medical care. In-home aides may not administer medications. They can only help clients self-administer [S2]. Aides who give extensive assistance must be listed on the Nurse Aide Registry under 10A NCAC 13J .1107(b). We saw that rule only on a mirror site, so verify it against the official text [S32]. Agencies must also document that their in-home caregivers are competent for assigned tasks [S5].

**Business model.** The agency employs aides, schedules them, and bills either the client (private pay) or Medicaid. Each site that provides home care must hold its own license [S1]. In-home aide services may be delivered only in contiguous counties or within 90 minutes' driving time of the agency site, so that supervision is possible [S2]. That rule effectively sets the service area for a one-office agency.

**Two regulatory layers.** The DHSR license (10A NCAC 13J) is the baseline for every agency. Medicaid billing adds a second layer: NC Medicaid Clinical Coverage Policy 3L for State Plan PCS (amended January 1, 2026), the CAP/DA waiver (CMS waiver 0132.R08.00) and electronic visit verification (EVV) [S12][S20][S15]. The Medicaid layer is covered in Section 4. This report does not cover Medicare-certified home health, which requires a Certificate of Need [S2].

**Rule stability.** The 2025 periodic review of 10A NCAC 13J listed no amendments [S7]. We found no proposed 2026 amendments to Subchapter 13J. An industry suggestion that agencies keep an NC-located premise was not adopted [S7]. Re-check the OAH site before filing.
sections.licensing_pathway:
**Step 1: Decide whether you need the license.** Aide, companion, sitter, respite or homemaker services delivered in a client's home are home care under G.S. 131E-136(3), and the license is mandatory [S2]. Each site providing home care must be separately licensed [S1].

**Step 2: Form the business.** Form the legal entity and obtain an EIN before applying. An LLC filing fee of about $125 and an annual report fee of about $200 appeared only in secondary sources. We did not verify them on the NC Secretary of State site, so confirm both before filing. North Carolina has no statewide general business license, but local governments may require business privilege licenses (secondary source, not verified). We did not verify zoning or siting rules for a home care office.

**Step 3: Complete the pre-licensure requirement.** The application packet must include proof of previously owning and operating a home care agency, **or** proof of completion of DHSR home care provider training [S1]. Under 10A NCAC 13J .0903, the Division does not issue a license until an applicant without that history has received Division-approved training [S6][S2]. The cost of the training was not found.

**Step 4: Meet the director qualification.** The agency director must be one of the following [S4]:

- a licensed health care practitioner;
- a person with at least two years of supervisory or management experience in home care or another provider licensed under G.S. 131E or G.S. 122C; or
- a person with a bachelor's degree in health, business or public administration science plus at least one year of supervisory or management experience in home care or another licensed health care program.

An agency licensed only for companion, sitter and respite services has a lighter director standard: high school or GED, plus a health care practitioner license or one year of experience. If the director position becomes vacant, DHSR must be notified in writing within five working days [S4].

**Step 5: File the application and fee.** The steps are, in order, the licensure application, the fee, proof of experience or training, and mailing the packet to DHSR [S1].

- The **initial fee is $510** and is nonrefundable [S3].
- It is paid with the signed application packet (check, money order or certified check payable to the N.C. Division of Health Service Regulation), not after approval [S1].
- Mail: Acute and Home Care Licensure section, 2712 Mail Service Center, Raleigh, NC 27699. Phone 919-855-4620. Email DHSR.homecare@dhhs.nc.gov [S1][S2].

**Step 6: Initial review and survey.** DHSR emails a confirmation after receipt and then requests policies, procedures and personnel documents. The **initial survey is a document review** [S1].

**Timeline.** DHSR states that it is not possible to establish specific time frames, because completeness, requests for more information and surveyor workload vary [S2]. The applicant must complete all requirements within one year (12 months) of DHSR receiving the application and fee [S1]. Secondary sites cite 60 to 90 day timelines, which contradict the official statement and are not used here.

**License term and renewal.** Licensure runs to midnight on December 31 whenever it was issued, so do not assume a 12-month term [S6][S2]. A license issued mid-year needs a second **$510 renewal fee** received by that December 31, within months of the first payment. The renewal application and fee must be received by December 31 [S2][S3]. A renewal received after January 1 takes effect only on the date received, which leaves a gap in licensure. All fees are nonrefundable. The license must be posted in a prominent location in the premises accessible to public view [S5].

**Changes.** A change of ownership or name needs written notice to DHSR at least 30 days before it takes effect [S5]. A change of ownership carries a $510 fee [S3].

**Inspections.** Inspections and complaint investigations are unannounced [S2]. Inspections occur about every three years [S2]. The agency must allow immediate access to its premises and records [S5]. Cited deficiencies require a plan of correction; confirm the deadline in the survey report or with DHSR.

**Medicaid enrollment.** Licensure does not enroll you with Medicaid. NC Medicaid charges a mandatory **$100** provider application fee on initial enrollment, and a federal application fee of **$750** applies for calendar year 2026. Confirm in the Provider Permission Matrix that the federal fee applies to your taxonomy. Both fees are paid with the application before processing and are due again at re-verification and for each added site. Confirm current enrollment steps (NCTracks forms, site visit timing) with NC Medicaid before budgeting.
sections.reimbursement:
**How money flows.** North Carolina home care revenue comes through two channels. Private-pay clients pay the agency directly by the hour. Medicaid pays for personal care that has been authorized under State Plan PCS or a waiver.

**Private pay.** CareScout's 2025 Cost of Care Survey lists North Carolina's median non-medical in-home caregiver rate at **$30 per hour** [S23]. The annual and monthly figures ($68,640 and $5,720) assume 44 hours per week for 52 weeks, with rates collected July to November 2025 [S23]. The 2025 survey merged the former homemaker and home health aide categories into one line. The 2024 survey showed $30 for each category [S24]. A secondary, non-government overview reports statewide agency personal-care rates of $24 to $35 per hour with wide regional variation [S25]. Treat $30 as a statewide median to test against local competitors, not a price guarantee.

**State Plan PCS.** State Plan PCS in in-home settings is governed by Clinical Coverage Policy 3L, amended January 1, 2026. The provider must obtain a service authorization for a specified number of PCS hours per month and have an approved service plan [S12].

**The August 2026 rate increase.** Effective August 1, 2026, NC Medicaid's Division of Health Benefits applied an **18% increase** to current PCS procedure-code rates [S8].

- It covers PCS delivered through NC Medicaid Direct and the CAP/C, CAP/DA and CAP/CD waivers [S9].
- State Plan PCS code 99509 (HA, HB) rose from $5.96 to **$7.03** per unit, and CAP/C code S5125 rose from $5.96 to $7.03 [S9].
- The 2026 Appropriations Act (S.B. 257) provided $70.8 million in recurring state funding for PCS rate increases [S9].
- The July 31 bulletin was superseded in full by the August 4 update [S8][S9].

**Managed care.** Alliance Health, a Tailored Plan, loaded the increased PCS rate with an August 1, 2026 effective date and began billing on August 4, 2026. It re-adjudicates prior claims, and the billing rate is $7.03 per unit [S10]. Other plans' rates and contract terms were not verified. Each plan's contract governs, and plan-contracted PCS providers must use the plan's EVV solution rather than the state's [S18].

**Unit length (an open item).** The bulletin table gives a rate per unit without defining the unit. The model reads it as 15 minutes ($7.03 × 4 = $28.12 per hour). Two points support that reading. First, S.B. 896 describes the PCS rate as being per 15-minute increment [S34]. Second, the CY2025 CAP/DA in-home aide disclosure shows an average of **$23.85 per hour** across 13,513,759 units and 8,216 beneficiaries [S22], and that figure is about four times the pre-increase $5.96 unit rate. It is still an inference. Confirm the unit and the CAP/DA code-level rate on the NC Medicaid fee schedule before relying on the Medicaid configurations. The $23.85 figure is a pre-increase average from rates in effect on July 1, 2025, and is not a current fee-schedule rate [S22].

**CAP/DA.** The renewed CAP/DA 1915(c) waiver runs November 1, 2024 through October 31, 2029 [S13]. It includes a personal care aide service [S14]. CAP/DA is capped by slots, and waitlists form when slots are full (Section 5) [S21].

**Pending or unverified rate actions (not assumed in the model).**

- S.B. 896 would raise the PCS rate to $7.50 per 15-minute increment. Only its filing on April 29, 2026 was confirmed [S34].
- SPA 26-0007 (PCS rates) has a one-day public notice dated July 28, 2026 [S33].
- A 'Medicaid Rates Revised FY27 – October 2026' listing appears on a managed care provider page [S10]. We saw it as a listing only and did not verify its content.

**EVV and payment risk.** EVV is required for Medicaid PCS and CAP/DA under the 21st Century Cures Act [S15]. NC Medicaid says providers should capture EVV data electronically at least 85% of the time, keeping manual entries to 15% or less [S16]. Sandata is NC Medicaid's procured vendor for NC Medicaid Direct services [S17]. Visits that do not reconcile with the EVV record create billing rework and cash-flow risk, and the model includes a per-client allowance for it.
sections.demand:
**Aging demographics.** North Carolina had 2,038,854 residents aged 65 and older in 2025 (about 18% of the population), and the projection for 2050 is 2,996,376 [S30]. That is about 958,000 more people over 65 than in 2025. This is a long-run demand driver and not a measure of near-term client counts.

**Medicaid and waiver demand.** CAP/DA offers 18 home and community-based services and states a capacity of 11,648 recipients [S19]. We found an earlier official figure of 11,534. Another secondary source cites a higher number, and the conflict is unresolved, so the capacity is not claimed as current. In NC Medicaid's CY2025 rate disclosure, CAP/DA adult in-home aide services reached about **8,216 beneficiaries** [S22].

CAP/DA demand has exceeded slots. In a March 2024 notice, NC Medicaid stated that CAP/DA assessments rose significantly over the prior year, resulting in maximum utilization of the waiver slots, and that applicants may be waitlisted [S21]. NCLIFTSS manages CAP/DA referrals and assessments and can be reached at 833-522-5429 [S21]. The current statewide waitlist count was not retrieved. For an agency, the practical effect is that CAP/DA referrals are constrained by slot availability, while State Plan PCS and private pay do not have the same slot limit.

**Referral sources.** We found no official NC data on referral-source mix, agency utilization or private-pay market size, so none is claimed. Typical referral channels (hospital discharge planners, senior living communities, elder-law attorneys, health plans and families searching online) are operator assumptions to test locally. The model carries marketing and referral-development lines for them.

**Competition.** DHSR publishes a downloadable list of licensed home care, hospice, home health and nursing pool facilities, last updated August 20, 2026 [S31]. We did not parse it and claim no provider count. Before committing, download the list, filter to your county and contiguous counties, and count the licensed competitors there. The 90-minute service-area rule [S2] means your real market is the contiguous counties around your site.

**What we cannot say.** We have no verified NC market shares, named competitors, occupancy rates, or PCS beneficiary and unit counts by payer. Treat the demand case as directional and validate it with local discharge planners, senior services and a competitor price check.
sections.operations:
**Leadership and supervision.**

- **Agency director.** The director must be a licensed health care practitioner, or have two years of supervisory or management experience in home care or another G.S. 131E/122C provider, or hold a bachelor's degree in health, business or public administration science plus one year of supervisory or management experience [S4]. Companion, sitter and respite-only agencies have a lighter standard (high school or GED plus a health care practitioner license or one year of experience). If the position becomes vacant, notify DHSR in writing within five working days [S4].
- **RN.** An RN must be continuously available for supervision and consultation during all hours in-home aide services are provided, and able to go on-site [S2]. The agency RN must also conduct a home visit to make observations, collect data and develop the plan of care [S2].
- **Supervisory visits.** Rule 10A NCAC 13J .1110 requires a supervisory visit to each client's residence every 90 days, with or without the caregiver present, and annually while the caregiver is providing care. The agency policy sets the method and frequency for other caregiver types. Medicaid CCP 3L service-plan requirements are separate.
- **LPNs.** An LPN may not perform assessments or conduct supervisory visits for in-home aide services [S2].

The models therefore carry an RN, an after-hours or relief RN allowance, and a director. At the 20-client size a single owner can fill the director and RN roles if she or he is a licensed RN. A licensed health care practitioner qualifies as director [S4]. A solo owner-RN has no legal backup for illness, leave, nights and weekends, so a relief or PRN RN is also needed to stay compliant.

**Aide staffing.** In-home aides may not administer medications [S2]. Aides doing extensive assistance must be on the Nurse Aide Registry (mirror text, verify) [S32]. The agency must document each aide's competency for assigned tasks [S5]. We found no official rule text for aide staffing ratios, initial aide training hours, or required annual in-service hours. The DHSR FAQ says the agency sets in-service hours in its own policy without giving a number [S2]. The training line in the model is an operator estimate. Federal overtime rules apply: third-party home care employers cannot use the FLSA companionship or live-in exemption, so hours over 40 a week are paid at 1.5x. Schedule accordingly.

**Hiring and background checks.** Under G.S. 131E-265, the agency must submit the criminal history check request within five business days of a conditional offer of employment [S2]. An agency may not hire anyone with a substantiated finding on the Health Care Personnel Registry (10A NCAC 13J .1003(c)). Registry questions go to 919-855-3968 [S2]. Fees for these checks were not found, so the model's check cost is an operator estimate.

**Service area.** Aides may serve only clients in contiguous counties or within 90 minutes' driving time of the site [S2]. A second office needs its own license [S1].

**Records and inspections.** Inspections are unannounced and the agency must grant immediate access to premises and records [S2][S5]. Keep client files, service plans, RN visit notes, aide competency records and personnel files inspection-ready at all times. Post the license in a publicly visible place [S5].

**Medicaid operations (if enrolling).** Each authorization needs a service plan under CCP 3L [S12]. Every Medicaid PCS and CAP/DA visit needs EVV, with at least 85% of visit data captured electronically [S15][S16]. Plan-contracted providers use the plan's EVV solution, while NC Medicaid Direct visits use the state vendor Sandata [S17][S18]. Budget for a coordinator who reconciles EVV, authorizations and claims.

**Payroll and employer accounts.** The 2026 NC unemployment insurance taxable wage base is $34,200 per employee, the beginning-employer rate is 1.0%, and experience-rated rates range from 0.06% to 5.76% [S29]. Workers' compensation class code and rate for home care were not retrieved. The model's 5% is an operator estimate, so get quotes. Required insurance minimums for a home care agency were also not retrieved.
sections.market_conditions:
**Wages.** No NC-specific BLS OEWS wage for home health or personal care aides was retrieved. The benchmarks we do have:

- The North Carolina median for personal care aides (SOC 31-1120) is about **$15.02 per hour** ($31,240 a year; 10th percentile $11.87, 90th percentile $18.60) per the NC Careers occupation profile. The vintage of that figure is not stated. The model now uses it for aides. Confirm against BLS OEWS for NC.
- The national median wage for home health and personal care aides was **$35,800 per year (about $17.21 per hour)** in May 2025 [S27]. The earlier model run used it, and it serves as a high-side sensitivity.

The NC minimum wage is **$7.25 per hour** in 2026 [S28], so every modeled wage is well above the floor. We found no local minimum wage in NC metros, but preemption was reported only by secondary sources and we did not verify it. Director, RN and coordinator salaries in the models are operator estimates. A secondary Charlotte RN range of $30 to $38 per hour supported the $78,000 RN figure, but it is not an official wage. Verify all of these locally.

**Employer tax environment.** NC's 2026 UI taxable wage base is $34,200, the beginning-employer rate is 1.0% and the experience-rated range is 0.06% to 5.76% [S29].

**Private-pay pricing.** The CareScout NC median is $30 per hour [S23], the same as in the 2024 survey [S24]. Some secondary sources report a $24 to $35 range [S25]. The $30 figure covers a merged homemaker and home health aide category and is a statewide median. It may not match the Charlotte, Raleigh or rural markets you serve.

**Medicaid rates.** The 18% PCS increase in August 2026 moved State Plan PCS and CAP/C to $7.03 per unit [S8]. It lifts Medicaid per-hour revenue from $23.84 to $28.12 on the 15-minute reading, which is close to the private-pay median. A further increase to $7.50 per unit is only a filed bill [S34], and an October 2026 FY27 rate revision is listed but unverified [S10]. Do not assume either.

**Supply and facilities.** The licensed provider count is not claimed (Section 5). Rent benchmarks by NC metro were not verified. HUD's FY2026 national non-metropolitan reference rent is $973 per month, which is a residential 2-bedroom reference and not an office benchmark. The office lease lines in the models are operator estimates and should be replaced with local quotes.

**Policy watch-list.**

- the 10A NCAC 13J rules appear stable [S7];
- S.B. 896 (proposed higher PCS rate) [S34];
- the SPA 26-0007 notice [S33];
- the October 2026 FY27 rate revision listing [S10];
- CAP/DA slot and waitlist changes [S21].
sections.financial_narrative:
**How the model is built.** Revenue per client is rate × hours (or units) × payer share. Costs are aide wages, the leadership team the rules require, and fixed and per-client operating costs. Rent and utilities are fixed. Per-client lines cover software, liability exposure, background checks, recruiting, supplies, mileage, billing rework, and payment processing on private-pay invoices. Payroll burden is 17% (9% payroll tax, 5% workers' comp, 3% benefits) with no overtime allowance; the model assumes no aide exceeds 40 hours a week, and overtime at 1.5x would add cost (a 3–6% allowance on aide wages is a sensible sensitivity). Workers' comp and benefits are operator estimates, and the tax component uses the 2026 NC beginning-employer UI rate [S29]. Occupancy is 90% by default, with 85% and 95% as conservative and optimistic cases. These are operator assumptions, not NC data.

Key assumptions: **80 billable hours per client per month** (about 18 per week), plus 4% paid non-billable time; a **$15.02 NC aide median** from NC Careers (vintage not stated; NC OEWS not retrieved), which replaces the $17.21 national median [S27] used in the earlier run; and a $30 private-pay price [S23]. The hours figure is an operator estimate, set well below the 44-hour/week basis of the CareScout price [S23]. Verify the hours, the non-billable share, and the aide wage locally.

**Status of the results.** The table below comes from the earlier run at the **$17.21 national wage** (and, for the 20-client model, a $300 on-call stipend). It is a high-side sensitivity. It has not yet been re-run at the NC wage, the larger relief-RN allowance for the 20-client owner-RN model, or an overtime allowance. A rough independent recompute of the 60-client case also differed from the $5,177 shown, so treat all of these figures as provisional.

**Earlier run at $17.21, 90% occupancy:**

| Configuration | Net per month | Margin | Break-even occupancy | First profitable month | Cash needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Private pay, 60 clients (default) | $5,177 | 4.0% | 75.7% | 13 | $194,278 |
| Medicaid, 100 clients | $5,640 | 2.8% | 78.4% | 15 | $311,865 |
| Mixed 60 (50% private / 50% Medicaid) | $2,039 | 1.6% | 83.8% | 15 | $213,106 |
| Private pay, 40 clients | −$2,353 | −2.7% | 99.8% | none | $245,472 |
| Private pay, 20 clients (RN owner) | −$2,364 | −5.5% | 109.6% | none | $144,775 |

Cash needed includes start-up costs and the modeled ramp-up deficit, not the advisory working-capital range.

**Effect of the NC wage.** Moving from $17.21 to $15.02 lowers aide cost by about $213 per client-month with burden. At 54 clients that is about $11,500 per month, and about $7,700 per month at 36 clients. That is larger than the 60-client profit above and would change the 20- and 40-client loss results. The full re-run is needed before any of these figures are used for a decision.

**Why scale matters (earlier $17.21 run).** A private client at 80 hours bills $2,400 per month. Aide cost with burden was about $1,675, and per-client costs are about $123, so each client contributed roughly **$600 per month**. At 54 clients (60 at 90% occupancy) that is about $32,500 per month, against fixed costs of about $27,300. Fixed costs are the director, RN and coordinators (about $19,800 loaded) plus rent, insurance, marketing and other fixed costs (about $7,500). That left the $5,177 shown. Break-even sat at about 45 clients. The 40-client model has nearly the same leadership team spread over fewer clients. The 20-client RN-owner model lost about $28,400 a year after a $72,000 owner salary in that run. That is a statement of the arithmetic, not a recommended draw.

**Sensitivities on the default (60-client private-pay) model, at 54 clients.** The dollar figures below are from the earlier $17.21 run. The NC wage shifts them upward by roughly $11,500 per month.

- **Aide wage.** Each $1.00 per hour changes net by about $5,260 per month ($97 per client-month with burden). With other inputs unchanged, the default breaks even at an aide wage near $18.20 per hour. The wage is the most sensitive input, and the NC figure is an unconfirmed operator input.
- **Price.** Each $1.00 per hour of bill rate changes net by about $4,320 per month. Raising the price in the model is not a fix. Test your local market's actual price before assuming any rate above the statewide median.
- **Hours per client.** Each billable hour contributes about $9 after aide cost and burden at $17.21 (about $11 at $15.02). Each 10 fewer hours per client-month lowers net by about $4,900 at the earlier wage. This is an operator-estimate sensitivity.
- **Occupancy.** Break-even was 75.7% of 60 clients, about 45 clients, in the earlier run. Below break-even the agency loses money every month.

**Medicaid (earlier $17.21 run).** At $7.03 per 15-minute unit ($28.12 per hour) and 80 hours, a Medicaid client contributed about $487 per month, which is less than a private client. The shortfall is about $150 per client-month at the same hours, because $28.12 is below $30. The 100-client Medicaid model earned about $5,640 per month only through scale (90 clients), with the lowest margin of the profitable options and the highest cash need. The mixed 60-client model earned less than the private-only 60 because half the clients pay less per hour and EVV, billing and rework add cost.

Two Medicaid cautions:

- **Rate.** At the earlier wage, the 100-client Medicaid model broke even at about **$6.83 per unit**, roughly $0.20 below the current $7.03. Each $0.10 per unit moves net by about $2,900 per month at 90 clients. At the pre-increase $5.96 the model would lose heavily. S.B. 896's $7.50 would add roughly $13,500 per month but is only filed and is not assumed [S34].
- **Hours.** The CY2025 CAP/DA disclosure implies about 137 units per beneficiary per month (13,513,759 ÷ 8,216 ÷ 12) [S22]. On the 15-minute reading that is about 34 hours, not the modeled 80, though beneficiaries may not all be enrolled for twelve months and the unit is unconfirmed. At 137 units the contribution per client falls to roughly $160 per month, and the modeled team would be badly oversized. Validate real authorized hours before building a Medicaid-heavy agency.

**Metro wages.** Larger NC metros may price labor above the NC median. If your aide wage is above about $18.20, the default model is at or below break-even with other inputs unchanged.
sections.risks:
**Thin margins.** The best margins in the earlier $17.21 run were 4.0% (private pay, 60 clients) and 2.8% (Medicaid, 100 clients). A small shift in aide wage, billable hours, price or occupancy can turn the default into a loss (Section 8). In that run the 20- and 40-client private-pay models lost money, but the NC wage change would materially improve them. The figures have not yet been re-run.

**Unverified wage and cost inputs.** The aide wage ($15.02) is the NC Careers median with an unstated vintage, and the NC OEWS value was not retrieved. The national median is $17.21 [S27]. The director, RN and coordinator salaries, rent, insurance, workers' comp, training and background-check costs are operator estimates. We found no official NC data for them, and local wages may differ. No overtime allowance is modeled, although hours over 40 a week must be paid at 1.5x.

**Unverified Medicaid inputs.**

- The PCS unit length is inferred as 15 minutes, and the CAP/DA code-level rate was not verified [S8][S22].
- Managed care plan terms were not independently confirmed [S10].
- Authorized hours per client may be well below the modeled 80 [S12][S22].
- Medicaid enrollment budgets assume a $100 NC fee plus a $750 federal fee for 2026; confirm the federal fee applies to your taxonomy.

**Rate and policy change.** S.B. 896, SPA 26-0007 and an October 2026 FY27 rate revision are pending or unverified [S33][S34][S10]. Rates can rise or fall, and the 2026 increase was legislatively funded [S8].

**CAP/DA slots and waitlists.** CAP/DA slots are capped and have reached maximum utilization in the past [S21]. Referrals are constrained by slots, and the current waitlist and capacity are unverified.

**Payment timing and EVV.** Medicaid visits need EVV with at least 85% electronic capture, and plan-contracted providers use plan-specific EVV [S16][S18]. Mismatched visits create denials and rework. Medicaid agencies carry the highest cash need (about $311,865 in the earlier run).

**Regulatory risk.**

- **RN availability.** An RN must be continuously available whenever aides are working [S2]. A single-RN agency has coverage gaps, so the models carry an on-call allowance, and the 20-client owner-RN model carries a relief RN allowance.
- **Supervisory visits.** Rule .1110 requires a supervisory visit every 90 days and annually while care is provided.
- **Director vacancy.** DHSR must be notified within five working days [S4].
- **Unannounced surveys.** Surveys are unannounced, and deficiencies require a plan of correction [S2].
- **Hiring bars.** Background-check timing and Health Care Personnel Registry hiring bars create hiring risk [S2].
- **Licensing delay and renewal gap.** DHSR gives no processing time frame, so budget for the full 12-month completion window, and training is required if you lack prior ownership [S1][S2][S6]. Licenses expire Dec. 31, and a late renewal creates a gap in licensure.
- **Service area.** The 90-minute and contiguous-county limit caps geographic growth [S2].
- **Rules.** Subchapter 13J is under periodic review [S7].

**Wage-pressure risk.** The NC minimum wage is $7.25 [S28], but market wages for aides are far higher, and metro labor markets may price above the NC median. We did not verify whether any city or county sets a higher minimum.

**Insurance and legal exposure.** We found no official insurance, bond or auto-liability minimums. Plans and clients may require limits, so obtain quotes. Workers' comp class code and rate were not retrieved.

**Data caveats.** Several pages were retrieved only as search excerpts. Re-check quotes against live pages before publication, and treat secondary sources (CareScout summaries, Senior IDY [S25], the 10A NCAC 13J .1107 mirror [S32]) as less reliable than official ones.
sections.recommendations:
1. **Plan for the 60-client private-pay model, not the 20- or 40-client versions, until the model is re-run.** It is the default and was the only private-pay configuration that earned a profit in the earlier $17.21 run ($5,177 per month, break-even near 75.7%, first profitable month 13). Smaller agencies lost money under the staffing the rules require, but the NC wage would improve every configuration, so re-run all five before deciding. If you start smaller, run it as a pre-launch stage with a deliberately lean fixed cost. An RN owner-director who covers the director and RN roles [S4][S2] is the cheapest way to meet the rules, but budget a relief RN for illness, leave and off-hours.

2. **Fund the ramp.** The default needed about $194,000 of cash in the earlier run (start-up costs plus the modeled ramp deficit) and 13 months to a first profitable month. A Medicaid-focused agency needed about $312,000. Re-run these at the NC wage, and do not launch without the full amount plus a cushion for slower admissions.

3. **Price locally.** Use the $30 statewide median [S23] only as a starting point. Check what licensed competitors in your counties charge (use the DHSR facility list [S31]). Each $1.00 per hour changes net by about $4,300 per month at 54 clients, but do not assume a higher price in the plan.

4. **Control the two biggest variables: aide wage and billable hours.** The model uses the NC Careers median of about $15.02 per hour, whose vintage is not stated. Confirm the NC OEWS and local wage before finalizing the plan, because every $1.00 per hour moves net by about $5,300 per month. Build a recruiting and scheduling process that delivers at least 70 to 80 billable hours per client per month, track travel and non-billable time from day one, and schedule so aides do not exceed 40 hours a week without 1.5x pay.

5. **Add Medicaid only after the office is paid for, and only after verifying the inputs.**
   - Confirm the PCS unit length and the CAP/DA code-level rate on the NC Medicaid fee schedule.
   - Confirm typical authorized hours per client under CCP 3L [S12].
   - Budget the $100 NC and $750 federal (2026) enrollment fees, confirm the federal fee applies to your taxonomy, and confirm the contract terms and EVV requirements with each managed care plan [S10][S18].
   - Medicaid clients contribute about $150 per month less than private clients at the same hours, so the case for Medicaid is volume, not margin.
   - Do not build the plan on S.B. 896 [S34] or the unverified FY27 revision [S10].

6. **Build compliance in from the start.**
   - Complete the DHSR-approved training before or alongside the application if you have no prior home care ownership [S6].
   - Pay the $510 fee with the application packet [S1][S3].
   - Prepare policies, procedures and personnel files for the document-based initial survey [S1].
   - Licenses expire Dec. 31 whatever the issue date. Set a renewal reminder and budget a second $510 payment in year one if you are licensed mid-year [S2].
   - Keep an RN available for all aide hours, and schedule supervisory visits at least every 90 days under .1110 [S2].
   - Run criminal history requests within five business days and screen the Health Care Personnel Registry before hiring [S2].
   - Keep inspection-ready files [S2][S5].

7. **Verify before launch.** Get quotes for liability, auto and workers' compensation insurance and check any plan or client insurance requirements. Verify zoning and local business licensing for your office. Confirm LLC filing and annual report fees with the NC Secretary of State. Pull NC and local BLS wage data, and check whether any local minimum wage applies.

8. **Re-run the model now and quarterly.** Update the PCS rate, wage, price, hours and occupancy against actuals. Move to the Medicaid or mixed model only if the verified inputs show a better contribution than the private-pay base.

checklist.task: Confirm that your services require a NC Home Care Agency license
checklist.instructions: In-home aide, companion, sitter, respite and homemaker services all count as home care under G.S. 131E-136(3). Operating without a license is prohibited. Read the DHSR 'Requirements for Establishing a Home Care Agency' page and the Home Care FAQ before spending money. Time: 1 day.

checklist.task: Decide the business model and size using the bundle's financial model
checklist.instructions: At the modeled assumptions (90% census, $30/hour private pay, 80 hours per client-month), the 60-client private-pay agency nets about $5,177/month (4.0% margin) and breaks even near 75.7% occupancy. The 40-client and 20-client private-pay agencies lose money at 90% census. Do not open at a size your cash cannot carry: modeled cash needs run from about $145,000 to $312,000 depending on configuration. All hours-per-client and wage inputs are operator estimates, so verify them locally.

checklist.task: Form a North Carolina legal entity (e.g., LLC)
checklist.instructions: File Articles of Organization with the NC Secretary of State. A secondary source reports a $125 filing fee, but the SOS fee page was not verified, so confirm the current fee at sosnc.gov before filing. Time: typically days. Choose the entity name before filing the DHSR application, because the licensee name must match.

checklist.task: Obtain a federal EIN
checklist.instructions: Apply free at irs.gov. You need it for payroll, banking, NC withholding and unemployment accounts, and Medicaid (NCTracks) enrollment. Time: same day online.

checklist.task: Open a business bank account and set up bookkeeping
checklist.instructions: Keep agency funds separate from personal funds. Use accounting software that can produce payer-level (private pay vs. Medicaid) revenue reports. Budget about $600–$1,300/month for accounting, payroll service and legal depending on size (operator estimate per configuration).

checklist.task: Register with the NC Division of Employment Security (unemployment insurance)
checklist.instructions: Open an employer account before the first payroll. For 2026 a beginning employer is assigned a 1.0% rate on the first $34,200 of each employee's wages. After the initial period (a secondary source says two years) the rate moves to experience rating, with a 2026 range of 0.06%–5.76%. Time: 1–2 days online.

checklist.task: Register for NC withholding and confirm other state tax obligations
checklist.instructions: Register with the NC Department of Revenue for withholding before the first payroll. Confirm requirements with your accountant. The NC DOR and Secretary of State pages were not verified in this research.

checklist.task: Check local business license, zoning and signage rules for your office
checklist.instructions: NC has no statewide general business license, but cities and counties often require a local privilege license. Zoning or siting rules for home care offices were not verified in this research. Call the city/county planning office before signing a lease or using a home office. DHSR requires a public-facing sign at the door, so confirm that is allowed.

checklist.task: Choose and secure the physical agency site (one license per site)
checklist.instructions: Each site providing home care services must be separately licensed, and each agency premises needs its own license. Pick the site where you will hold records and supervise staff. Rent is a fixed cost: the model uses about $900/month (20 clients) to $3,000/month (100 clients) as operator estimates, because no NC metro rent benchmark was verified. Get a lease quote before committing.

checklist.task: Buy general/professional liability, hired-and-non-owned auto, crime/bond and workers' compensation insurance
checklist.instructions: No official NC insurance minimum for home care agencies was found, so get quotes and check what payer contracts, clients and referral sources require. The model uses $600/month base plus $15 per client (operator estimate) and a 5% workers' comp load on payroll. The NC class code and rate were not retrieved; ask your broker. Bind coverage before the first caregiver visits a client.

checklist.task: Qualify your agency director under one of the three paths
checklist.instructions: The director must be (a) a licensed health care practitioner, (b) have at least two years of supervisory or management experience in home care or another provider licensed under G.S. 131E or 122C, or (c) hold a bachelor's degree plus one year of that experience. Document the qualification in a personnel file. If the director position becomes vacant, notify DHSR in writing within five working days.

checklist.task: Complete DHSR-approved home care provider training (unless you have prior home care ownership/operation)
checklist.instructions: If you cannot show that you previously owned and operated a home care agency, DHSR will not issue the license until you receive Division-approved training. Contact DHSR (919-855-4620; DHSR.homecare@dhhs.nc.gov) for current training dates. The training cost was not found; the model allows $0–$500 as an operator estimate.

checklist.task: Download the current home care licensure application from DHSR
checklist.instructions: Get the application packet from the DHSR Acute and Home Care Licensure and Certification Section page ('Requirements for Establishing a Home Care Agency'). The DHSR page itself carries an old last-modified date, so ask the Section to confirm the form is current. Read the FAQ (rev. 5/30/25) alongside it.

checklist.task: Complete and sign the licensure application
checklist.instructions: Use the exact legal entity name and site address. Confirm the service area is within contiguous counties or within 90 minutes' driving time of the agency site, since in-home aide services may only be delivered there so that supervision is possible. Time: 1–3 days.

checklist.task: Pay the $510 initial licensure fee with the application packet
checklist.instructions: The fee is $510.00 and nonrefundable. Pay by check, money order or certified check payable to the N.C. Division of Health Service Regulation. It is sent together with the signed application, not after approval. Keep a copy of the check.
checklist.cite: DHSR Fee Schedule; DHSR licensure page

checklist.task: Attach proof of prior home care ownership OR proof of completed DHSR training
checklist.instructions: Include one of the two proofs in the packet. This is Step 3 of the DHSR process, between paying the fee and mailing.

checklist.task: Mail the complete packet to DHSR
checklist.instructions: Send it to the Acute and Home Care Licensure and Certification Section, 2712 Mail Service Center, Raleigh, NC 27699. Use trackable mail. Questions go to 919-855-4620 or DHSR.homecare@dhhs.nc.gov.

checklist.task: Watch the 12-month completion window
checklist.instructions: You must complete all licensing requirements within 12 months of DHSR's receipt of the application and fee. DHSR says it cannot publish specific processing time frames because completeness, extra information requests and surveyor workload vary. Do not sign long leases or hire a full team assuming a fixed approval date.

checklist.task: Respond to DHSR's confirmation email and policy/personnel request
checklist.instructions: After receipt, DHSR emails a confirmation, then requests policies, procedures and personnel documents. Reply promptly and keep a log of what was sent and when. Missing documents are the usual cause of delay.

checklist.task: Pass the document-based initial survey
checklist.instructions: DHSR conducts the initial survey by reviewing your policies, procedures and personnel documents for compliance. Prepare complete personnel files for the director, RN and any staff already hired. If deficiencies are cited, file a plan of correction within 10 working days of receipt.

checklist.task: Do not accept clients until the license is issued
checklist.instructions: Providing home care before licensure violates G.S. 131E-138. Use the waiting period to build policies, recruit and set up payers, but do not deliver or bill for services.

checklist.task: Confirm you are NOT seeking Medicare-certified home health
checklist.instructions: A Medicare-certified home health agency needs a Certificate of Need; a non-medical home care license does not. This bundle covers the home care license (in-home aide services) and Medicaid personal care only. Skilled nursing services would need different authority.

checklist.task: Check for rule changes before you file
checklist.instructions: The 2025 periodic review of 10A NCAC 13J marked every rule necessary and listed no amendments. No 2026 amendment was found, but recheck the OAH and DHSR pages the week you file. An industry suggestion that agencies keep an NC-located premise was not adopted.

checklist.task: Write the agency policy and procedure manual
checklist.instructions: Base it on 10A NCAC 13J (read the full subchapter). Cover client rights, intake, assessment and plan of care, supervision, in-home aide tasks, complaints, emergency procedures, confidentiality and personnel. Cost: your own time, or an operator-estimated $1,500–$5,000 for a consultant. Have it ready before DHSR requests it.

checklist.task: Define the scope of aide services and the medication limit in policy
checklist.instructions: In-home aides may not administer medications; they may only help clients self-administer. Write this into your policies and aide training. Keep the task list within what the rule permits for limited vs. extensive assistance.

checklist.task: Draft the plan-of-care process built around an RN home visit
checklist.instructions: The agency RN must make a home visit to make observations, collect data and develop the plan of care. An LPN may not perform assessments or supervisory visits for in-home aide services. Build visit templates, timelines and sign-off into the process.
checklist.cite: DHSR FAQ (plan of care; LPN limits)

checklist.task: Set up the RN supervision and consultation coverage schedule
checklist.instructions: An RN must be available for supervision and consultation during all hours that in-home aide services are provided. Document an on-call roster covering evenings and weekends. The model includes a $300–$900/month on-call stipend (operator estimate) on top of the RN salary.

checklist.task: Create the aide competency documentation system
checklist.instructions: Each agency must document that its in-home caregivers are competent for assigned tasks. Build competency checklists and sign-off records. The DHSR FAQ says the agency sets in-service hours in its own policy but gives no number, so choose a defensible annual number and follow it.

checklist.task: Check Nurse Aide Registry requirements for your aide task list
checklist.instructions: A mirror of 10A NCAC 13J .1107(b) says an aide who gives extensive assistance must be listed on the Nurse Aide Registry, and one who gives limited assistance need not be. This was seen only on a mirror site. Verify against the official OAH text and DHSR before deciding whether to hire only registry-listed aides.

checklist.task: Build the criminal history and Health Care Personnel Registry (HCPR) hiring process
checklist.instructions: Submit the criminal history check request within five business days of a conditional offer. Do not hire anyone with a substantiated finding on the HCPR (call 919-855-3968 with questions). Check fees were not found in official sources; the model uses $10 per client-month as an operator estimate.

checklist.task: Create personnel file templates
checklist.instructions: Include job description, qualification proof, HCPR and criminal check results, competency records, training and in-service records, and I-9. DHSR reviews personnel documents in the initial survey and any later inspection.

checklist.task: Prepare the client record and service agreement templates
checklist.instructions: Include the intake form, service agreement, rate and cancellation terms for private-pay clients, plan of care, aide task sheet, supervisory visit notes and complaint log. Have an attorney review the private-pay agreement.

checklist.task: Prepare for unannounced inspections and immediate access
checklist.instructions: All inspections and complaint investigations are unannounced, and the agency must allow immediate access to its premises and the records needed. Inspections occur about every three years. Keep records organized at the licensed site, with someone authorized to open them any business day.

checklist.task: Prepare license posting and door signage
checklist.instructions: After issuance, post the license in a prominent location accessible to public view within the premises, and post a sign at the public door as the rule requires. Check the exact sign wording in 10A NCC 13J .0903 and with DHSR.

checklist.task: Set up emergency, infection-control and incident-reporting procedures
checklist.instructions: Write procedures for client emergencies, aide no-shows, abuse/neglect reporting and incident documentation. Specific reporting time frames should be checked against 10A NCAC 13J and other applicable NC law, which were not fully reviewed here.

checklist.task: Hire or designate the agency director
checklist.instructions: Use the qualification paths in 10A NCC 13J .1001. In the model the owner-RN draws about $72,000 (20-client size) and a non-RN director about $65,000 (40+ clients); both are operator estimates. The Raleigh management group mean of $71.52/hour is an all-industry proxy, not a health-specific wage.

checklist.task: Hire a licensed RN supervisor (or confirm the owner-RN covers the role)
checklist.instructions: Verify the RN license is active with the NC Board of Nursing. The model uses about $78,000/year (about $37.50/hour) for a full-time RN, an operator estimate in line with a secondary Charlotte RN range of $30–$38/hour. One RN per roughly 60 clients is an operator estimate; Medicaid-heavy agencies need more (1.5 FTE at 100 clients).
checklist.cite: DHSR FAQ (RN availability; RN home visit)

checklist.task: Hire a scheduler / intake / billing coordinator
checklist.instructions: The model uses $40,000/year per FTE (operator estimate): 0.5 FTE at 20 clients, 1 FTE at 40, 1.5 at 60 (or mixed), 3 at 100 Medicaid clients. Medicaid agencies need staff skilled in EVV reconciliation, authorizations and claims.

checklist.task: Set aide wages with local data, not only the model's $17.21
checklist.instructions: The model uses the national median for home health and personal care aides ($35,800/year, about $17.21/hour, May 2025). An NC-specific BLS aide wage was not retrieved; the Raleigh-Cary personal care and service group mean is $19.29/hour. NC's minimum wage is $7.25, so these are market-driven wages. Check local job postings and recompute your margin: at a $15.00 wage aide cost falls by roughly $215 per client-month.
checklist.cite: BLS OOH; BLS Raleigh-Cary OEWS; FRED

checklist.task: Recruit aides and keep a pipeline
checklist.instructions: Use job boards, community colleges, CNA programs and referrals. Budget about $25 per client-month for recruiting and onboarding (operator estimate). Plan for turnover: every hire needs a criminal history check, an HCPR check and competency documentation before client assignment.

checklist.task: Verify aide qualifications and competency before first assignment
checklist.instructions: Confirm training, any Nurse Aide Registry listing needed for the tasks assigned, and sign-off on competency for each task. Keep the records in the personnel file.

checklist.task: Enroll in payroll service and comply with wage-and-hour rules
checklist.instructions: Pay at or above $7.25/hour (NC minimum; local minimums are reported preempted, but that came from secondary sources only). Count travel time between clients and non-billable time correctly under federal law; the model adds 4% paid non-billable time as an operator estimate. Employer burden in the model is 17% (FICA 7.65%, unemployment, FUTA, 5% workers' comp estimate and 3% benefits).

checklist.task: Check E-Verify and other employer obligations as you grow
checklist.instructions: A secondary source says E-Verify becomes mandatory at 25 or more employees in NC. A home care agency with 40+ clients will pass that quickly. Confirm the threshold with NC DOL/DHS before reaching it.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ENROLLMENT, EVV & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Decide whether to serve Medicaid clients and when
checklist.instructions: Medicaid PCS has a strong 2026 rate and a pending-rate environment, but modeled margins are thin: the 100-client Medicaid agency nets about $5,640/month (2.8% margin) with break-even near 78.4% occupancy, and the mixed 60-client agency nets about $2,039/month (1.6%). Medicaid also needs the largest cash cushion (about $312,000 modeled for 100 clients). Launch private pay first if cash is limited.
checklist.cite: Bundle financial model; NC Medicaid rate notice

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ENROLLMENT, EVV & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Understand the Medicaid PCS pathways
checklist.instructions: State Plan PCS in in-home settings is governed by Clinical Coverage Policy 3L (amended Jan. 1, 2026). CAP/DA is a 1915(c) waiver (Nov. 1, 2024 – Oct. 31, 2029) for adults 18+ at risk of institutionalization and includes a personal care aide service. The program page lists PCS and the waivers under NC Medicaid's long-term care section. Read the policy end to end before enrolling.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ENROLLMENT, EVV & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Enroll as a Medicaid provider through NCTracks
checklist.instructions: Current NCTracks steps, forms and site-visit timing were not confirmed on an official page. Start at the NC Medicaid PCS provider page. Federal and NC enrollment application fees apply to some provider types; the amounts were not verified from official NC pages, so confirm the fee for your provider type at NCTracks before applying. The model allows $0–$850 for enrollment and credentialing (operator estimate). Home care license must be in hand first.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ENROLLMENT, EVV & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Confirm which payers pay PCS claims (NC Medicaid Direct vs. managed care plans)
checklist.instructions: PCS claims for Tailored Plan members go to the assigned plan rather than NCTracks (per a non-government guide). Alliance Health, a Tailored Plan, loaded the increased rate effective 8/1/2026 and began billing 8/4/2026. Contact each plan in your service area to credential; plan terms beyond Alliance's notice were not verified.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ENROLLMENT, EVV & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Load the correct Medicaid PCS rates and verify the unit length
checklist.instructions: Effective Aug. 1, 2026 NC Medicaid applied an 18% increase to PCS rates: State Plan PCS 99509 (HA/HB) and CAP/C S5125 went from $5.96 to $7.03 per unit. The bulletin does not state the unit length; the model reads it as 15 minutes ($28.12/hour), an inference supported by the CY2025 CAP/DA average of $23.85/hour. Confirm the unit and CAP/DA code on the NC Medicaid fee schedule before pricing anything.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ENROLLMENT, EVV & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Do not assume S.B. 896 or later rate changes
checklist.instructions: S.B. 896 (proposed $7.50 per 15-minute unit) was only filed on 2026-04-29; enactment was not confirmed. A one-day public notice for SPA 26-0007 (PCS rates, July 28, 2026) and a listing of 'Medicaid Rates Revised FY27 – October 2026' were seen but not verified. Check the NC Medicaid rate pages each quarter.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ENROLLMENT, EVV & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Set up Electronic Visit Verification (EVV)
checklist.instructions: The 21st Century Cures Act requires EVV for PCS and home health. NC Medicaid expects at least 85% of visit data captured electronically (manual entries 15% or less). Sandata is the state's vendor for NC Medicaid Direct. Plan-contracted PCS providers must use the plan's EVV solution, so you may run more than one. Budget $250–$400/month for scheduling/EVV-interface software plus per-client fees (operator estimates).

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ENROLLMENT, EVV & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Train staff to keep manual EVV edits at or below 15%
checklist.instructions: Teach aides clock-in/clock-out at the client's home, how to handle poor connectivity, and who approves edits. Run weekly exception reports so claims are not denied or recouped for mismatches. A billing/rework allowance of $10 per client-month is in the model (operator estimate).

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ENROLLMENT, EVV & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Learn the service authorization and service plan requirement
checklist.instructions: In-home PCS requires a service authorization for a specified number of hours per month and an approved service plan from the provider. Do not schedule beyond authorized hours. Track authorization start/end dates for each client.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ENROLLMENT, EVV & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Understand CAP/DA slot limits and the referral path
checklist.instructions: CAP/DA slots are capped and county waitlists have occurred, so referrals may be limited. Referrals and assessments run through NCLIFTSS (833-522-5429). Official capacity figures conflict (11,534 on an older page, 11,648 later), and no current waitlist count was retrieved. Do not build your census plan around CAP/DA alone.

checklist.phase: PHASE 5 — MEDICAID ENROLLMENT, EVV & PAYER SETUP
checklist.task: Plan for Medicaid cash-flow lag
checklist.instructions: Claims can be delayed or denied for EVV and authorization mismatches. The modeled working capital for Medicaid configurations is large. Arrange a line of credit or reserve before taking Medicaid clients, and consider that managed care plans may re-adjudicate claims after a rate change.

checklist.phase: PHASE 6 — PRIVATE-PAY PRICING, MARKETING & CLIENT ACQUISITION
checklist.task: Set private-pay rates using local market checks
checklist.instructions: CareScout's 2025 survey lists NC's median non-medical in-home rate at $30/hour ($5,720/month on 44 hours/week). The category merges homemaker and home health aide and is a statewide figure. A secondary source reports $24–$35/hour agency rates with wide regional variation. Call at least five local agencies. The model's break-even depends heavily on the rate.

checklist.phase: PHASE 6 — PRIVATE-PAY PRICING, MARKETING & CLIENT ACQUISITION
checklist.task: Build referral relationships
checklist.instructions: Target hospital discharge planners, rehab and senior living communities, elder-law attorneys, geriatric care managers and physician offices. NC's 65+ population was about 2.04 million in 2025 and is projected near 3.0 million by 2050, but no NC-specific agency occupancy or referral-volume data was found. Budget $1,200–$2,000/month for marketing at private-pay sizes (operator estimate).

checklist.phase: PHASE 6 — PRIVATE-PAY PRICING, MARKETING & CLIENT ACQUISITION
checklist.task: Create a website and compliant advertising
checklist.instructions: State clearly that you are a licensed home care agency, and do not advertise services you are not licensed or staffed to provide (e.g., skilled nursing or medication administration). Display your license number once issued. Budget $2,000–$8,000 for launch marketing (operator estimate).

checklist.phase: PHASE 6 — PRIVATE-PAY PRICING, MARKETING & CLIENT ACQUISITION
checklist.task: Define minimum hours, cancellation and payment terms
checklist.instructions: The model assumes 80 hours per client-month (about 18 hours/week), an operator estimate well below the survey's 44-hour/week pricing basis. Test it against real inquiries. Accept ACH and card; the model uses 1.5% blended processing cost.

checklist.phase: PHASE 6 — PRIVATE-PAY PRICING, MARKETING & CLIENT ACQUISITION
checklist.task: Explore long-term care insurance and VA payer options
checklist.instructions: Many private clients use LTC insurance reimbursement. Ask carriers what licensing and documentation they require and prepare invoices accordingly. VA program requirements were not researched here.

checklist.phase: PHASE 6 — PRIVATE-PAY PRICING, MARKETING & CLIENT ACQUISITION
checklist.task: Track the Medicaid policy changes that affect your referral base
checklist.instructions: New Medicaid rules begin Oct. 1, 2026 and Jan. 1, 2027, including work requirements for some expansion adults. Traditional Medicaid enrollees, including people with disabilities and low-income older adults, are reported as not subject to the work requirements. Monitor how this affects PCS and CAP/DA referrals.

checklist.task: Calendar the Dec. 31 license renewal
checklist.instructions: All home care licenses expire at midnight on December 31. The renewal application and the $510 fee must be received by DHSR no later than Dec. 31 so the January 1 effective date is kept. The fee is nonrefundable. Set reminders in October and file by early December.

checklist.task: Notify DHSR 30 days before any ownership or name change
checklist.instructions: A proposed change in ownership or name requires written notice to DHSR at least 30 days before the effective date. A change of ownership carries a $510 fee. Plan any sale, restructuring or rename accordingly.

checklist.task: Keep a standing plan-of-correction process
checklist.instructions: If DHSR cites deficiencies, you must file a plan of correction within 10 working days of receipt. Assign one person to receive survey results and track the deadline.

checklist.task: Perform RN supervision and document it
checklist.instructions: Keep records showing RN availability during all aide hours, plan-of-care home visits and supervisory visits. LPNs may not do assessments or supervisory visits for in-home aide services. Supervisory-visit frequency should be set by policy consistent with 10A NCAC 13J; the exact interval was not verified here.

checklist.task: Verify the director position stays filled
checklist.instructions: If the agency director position becomes vacant, DHSR must be notified in writing within five working days. Name a qualified backup director in advance.

checklist.task: Hold the aide service area within the allowed distance
checklist.instructions: In-home aide services may be delivered only in contiguous counties or within 90 minutes' driving time of the agency site. Screen intake addresses against this limit before accepting clients.

checklist.task: Run recurring HCPR and criminal history checks on hires
checklist.instructions: Run the criminal history request within five business days of each conditional offer, and do not employ anyone with a substantiated HCPR finding. Keep documentation in the personnel file for inspectors.

checklist.task: Maintain required training and in-service logs
checklist.instructions: Record director continuing education, aide in-service and competency reassessments. The model budgets $120–$400/month for training and documentation (operator estimate).

checklist.task: File annual entity reports and renew local licenses
checklist.instructions: A secondary source reports a $200 annual LLC report due April 15; confirm on the NC Secretary of State site. Renew any city/county privilege license. The model carries $30/month for these (operator estimate).

checklist.task: Add a license for each additional site before opening it
checklist.instructions: Each site providing home care must be separately licensed. Opening a branch means a new application and a new $510 fee, so model its cash needs separately.

checklist.task: Track census against break-even every month
checklist.instructions: The modeled default 60-client private-pay agency breaks even near 75.7% occupancy (about 45 clients) and first turns profitable around month 13 on the modeled ramp. The 40-client and 20-client private-pay models do not break even at 90% census, and the mixed and Medicaid configurations need about 84% and 78%. Use the Pro Forma and update it with actual numbers.

checklist.task: Fund the ramp-up cash deficit before launch
checklist.instructions: Modeled cash needed: about $144,775 (20-client RN-owner), $245,472 (40 clients), $194,278 (60 private-pay), $213,106 (mixed 60) and $311,865 (100 Medicaid). Hold this in cash or committed credit; the generic $40,000–$150,000 working-capital line is an advisory range only.

checklist.task: Reprice if local wages are higher than modeled
checklist.instructions: Aide wages drive most cost. If your local market requires $19+ (the Raleigh-Cary group mean is $19.29/hour), recompute margins; the 60-client model's 4.0% margin leaves little room. Never plan on a Medicaid rate or private-pay price you cannot confirm.

checklist.task: Monitor minimum wage legislation
checklist.instructions: NC's minimum wage is $7.25 (2026). A proposal (H.B. 353) would raise it to $18 by 2030 but was not enacted per the sources reviewed. Check the General Assembly site each session and stress-test payroll if it advances.
checklist.cite: FRED NC minimum wage; NC Budget & Tax Center brief

checklist.task: Reconcile Medicaid claims weekly
checklist.instructions: Match authorizations, EVV visits and billed units before submission, and track denials by reason. Repeated EVV mismatches or manual-entry rates above 15% invite payer scrutiny.

checklist.task: Re-verify unverified items before launch
checklist.instructions: Items not verified in this research: insurance minimums, workers' comp class code/rate, zoning, background check fees, NC Medicaid enrollment fees and steps, CAP/DA code-level rates, and the current number of licensed agencies. DHSR publishes a licensed-facility spreadsheet (updated Aug. 20, 2026) you can use to gauge local competition.

checklist.task: Review the full checklist and contacts with a NC healthcare attorney and CPA
checklist.instructions: Have counsel confirm licensure, employment and payer-contract terms, and have the CPA confirm tax registrations. Keep DHSR (919-855-4620) and HCPR (919-855-3968) contacts handy.
